newsitem.title: USA: GM, UAW resume talks to end parts plant strike.
newsitem.headline: GM, UAW resume talks to end parts plant strike.

text.p: Progress was reported in a three-day old General Motors Corp. parts plant strike Friday that has already forced the shutdown of six assembly plants, affecting more than 17,000 workers.
"We're hearing that we're close but that we're not quite there yet," said Jim Marcum, financial secretary for United Auto Worker Local 909 in Warren, Mich.
"It could go five minutes. It could go another five days," he said.
About 2,800 members of Local 909 walked off the job at midnight Tuesday when talks on a new three-year contract failed to produce an agreement by the strike deadline.
The plant makes automatic transmissions for many of GM's front-wheel drive cars and light trucks, as well as wheels and suspension control arms.

Union officials said Thursday that some progress has been made on staffing issues. The union reportedly wants the automaker to add between 250 and 400 jobs to make up for retirements and ease overtime burdens.

However, the two sides are still at odds over GM's desire to move production of wheels out of the Warren plant. Sources close to the talks said GM has offered to make up for the wheel work by moving torque converters, used in auto transmissions, into Warren. But that move means the torque production would be lost by GM's Buick city complex, which is also staffed by UAW workers.

The strike has the temporary shutdown of plants in Lansing, Orion Township, and Flint, Mich. Those plants make the Buick LaSabre, Buick Riviera, Oldsmobile Aurora, Oldsmobile Achieva, Oldsmobile Eighty Eight, Pontiac Grand Am and Bonneville, and Chevrolet Cavalier.

In addition, an assembly complex in Oshawa, Ontario, with two assembly lines shut down Friday morning. The facility produces the Chevrolet Lumina and Monte Carlo, and the Buick Park Avenue, Regal and Century sedans.

GM spokesman Tom Klipstine said there are not likely to be any more shutdowns until next week. Analysts said production at the Doraville, Ga., plant that supplies GM's new minivans to both the United States and Europe could be halted by Tuesday because of a shortage of transmissions.

GM's Fairfax, Kan., plant, which makes the hot-selling Pontiac Grand Prix and Oldsmobile Intrigue, could also be shut down Tuesday or Wednesday, said Mike Robinet, managing director of CSM Forecasting, an industry consultant in Farmington Hills, Mich.

Production at GM's pickup truck operations and additional car plants could be affected later next week. Dealers said Friday that any disruption of truck production could have a quick ripple effect on retail sales.

GM full-size pickup truck production was already down because of a three-month strike by workers at GM's Pontiac, Mich., plant. In addition, GM's North American production was down for two weeks earlier this month for its annual summer shutdown.

"Generally speaking, we're short of trucks," said Gerald Seiner, president a group of GM dealerships in Salt Lake City. "On the car side, it will take a little longer. Something that lasts a week or two probably won't affect retail sales," he said.

GM has been on a company-wide campaign to shrink its hourly work force by 12,000 to 15,000 through attrition to reduce costs and become more competitive. The automaker had about 215,000 UAW workers last year.
Union leaders, trying to protect jobs and put a halt to oursourcing, have resisted those efforts. The clash has lead to six strikes against GM this year, including the Warren work stoppage.
GM's stock fell $1.375 to $56.94 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading.
